chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Suleym al-Farra, from al-Hasan ibn Muslim, who said:

My maternal aunt narrated to me. She said, 'I was seated by the courtyard of the Ka'bah, when Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) came over. So when he saw me, he altered his course towards me. So he greeted me and he said: 'What makes you sit over here?' So I said, 'I am awaiting a slave of ours'. She said, 'So he said to me: 'Emancipate him'. I said, 'No, but we have emancipated his father'. So he said: 'That is not your slave. This is your brother, and a son of your uncle. But rather, the slave is the one upon whom the bounty flowed. So when it flowed upon his father and his grandfather, so he is a son of your uncle, and your brother'.

key_terms.مَوْلًى: Freedman or client; one who is under the patronage of another

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on the relationship between a freedman and his master if only the father was emancipated?
ai.summary: This narration from *Al-Kafi* highlights Imam al-Sadiq’s (peace be upon him) juridical distinction between *mawali* (freedmen) and *qaraba* (kin), clarifying that freeing the father does not create a master-client bond for the son but rather establishes familial kinship. This ruling underscores the Shia emphasis on the social elevation of freed slaves and the integration of their descendants into the family structure, reflecting the broader Islamic principle that emancipation is an act of divine grace that alters social status. The context of the encounter at the Ka'bah further emphasizes the public and authoritative nature of this legal clarification within the early Shia community.
